model.comments: High effort Claude Fable 5.1. Thinking is always on for Fable; depth is controlled by Anthropic's output_config.effort, which OpenRouter sets from reasoning.effort (its verbosity field maps to the same native field, so this equals the older opus-4.x verbosity convention).

prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Hex on a 11x11 board. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(me: list[tuple[int, int]], opp: list[tuple[int, int]], color: str) -> tuple[int, int]: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move. - `me` is a list of (row, col) tuples containing your stones. - `opp` is a list of (row, col) tuples containing the opponent's stones. - `color` is your color: `'b'` for black which tries to connect the top and bottom sides, and `'w'` for white which tries to connect the left and right sides. - Rows and columns are 0-indexed in `0..10`. - An empty cell is any coordinate not in `me` or `opp`. - Your goal is to connect your two opposing sides; the opponent tries to connect their two opposing sides. - Note that the board is a grid each individual cell is a hexagonal shape. Thus to know which cell is touching which other cell requires spatial reasoning to determine the winning lines. - Every stone not on the edge of the board is touching exactly 6 other stones (since they are hexagonal). - Two of those 6 stones are in the same row, two are in the top row, and two are in the bottom row. - Example: The stone located at (4, 1) is touching (4, 0) and (4, 2) - and to its bottom is touching (5, 1) and (5, 0) - and to its top is touching (3, 1) and (3, 2) - An easy way to determine the touching cells of cell (i, j) is all it's 8 neighbors except for (i-1, j-1) and (i+1, j+1) # Action / Return Format - Return a single move as a tuple `(row, col)`. - The chosen cell must be empty and within the board bounds. - There is no pass; always place a stone. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I'm working out the Hex adjacency rules for this 11x11 board, with black connecting top-to-bottom and white connecting left-to-right, and thinking about using a resistance-based evaluation approach to build a policy that stays fast enough for the time limit.

My plan: first check for immediate wins, then check if I need to block an opponent's winning move, and otherwise fall back to scoring candidate moves. For scoring, I'm considering building an electrical resistance model where each player's stones and empty cells form a circuit, solving the linear system for each candidate move to estimate connection strength since 121 nodes is small enough to solve quickly.

I set edge resistance between adjacent cells as the average of their node resistances, then solve the reduced Laplacian system with fixed boundary voltages to get the current and effective resistance between source and sink. To handle both colors symmetrically, I notice transposing the board swaps rows and columns while preserving the hex adjacency structure, so I can reuse the same resistance computation for white by transposing the grid first.

Checking performance, evaluating around 121 candidate moves with a couple of Laplacian solves each stays comfortably fast, so I could extend to a shallow 2-ply search where I rank my top candidate moves and consider the opponent's best replies among their top few options too, still keeping the total solve count manageable.

I'll cap opponent replies to a shared pool of ~10 candidates for each of my top 6 moves, keeping evaluations manageable with a time check as a safety net. I'll switch the scoring to a log-resistance difference and make sure the resistance calculation handles disconnected or fully-connected edge cases safely with BFS checks and fallback values before building out the actual resistance computation on the board.

I'm setting up the sink node at row 10 similarly, then building the graph Laplacian over all non-blocked cells plus source and sink, fixing source voltage to 1 and sink to 0 to solve for interior voltages and compute total current, giving resistance as R = 1/I. To avoid singular systems from disconnected components, I only include cells reachable from the source via BFS, since components connected to the source stay well-conditioned.

For performance, with roughly 121 nodes and 360 edges, doing this in Python for ~242 evaluations should run in well under a second, so I'll precompute neighbor lists to speed it up. I also want to add an opening-move heuristic: play center if the board is empty.

I should build in immediate win/block detection—checking each empty cell to see if it's a winning move for either player is cheap enough to do exhaustively. If the opponent has multiple disjoint winning threats, I'm likely lost regardless, so blocking just one is the best I can do. I'm also wondering whether the epsilon value for own-stone conductance is too small, since that could make the matrix ill-conditioned.

For the search structure, I'll implement 2-ply lookahead: for each candidate move I make, evaluate the opponent's best reply and take the minimum score, then pick the move that maximizes that. I'll fall back to 1-ply scoring if time runs out, budgeting around 0.7 seconds using a timer. To keep this efficient, I'll evaluate every empty cell from both my perspective and the opponent's perspective at the root, then only expand 2-ply search on a smaller candidate set—maybe the top 6 of my moves against the top 8 of the opponent's replies—to keep the total number of evaluations manageable.

Now I'm setting up the board representation and helper functions for the game state.

Still building resistance calculation...

I'm estimating the cost at roughly 0.3 seconds per evaluation, which is borderline, so I'm thinking about vectorizing with numpy: precomputing edge arrays, masking for reachability, and computing conductances directly instead of looping in Python, then extracting the submatrix for only the reachable nodes to avoid singularities.

Actually, doing a full BFS in Python would cost about the same as a plain loop, so instead I'm considering adding a tiny leak term to the diagonal of the Laplacian to avoid singular matrices altogether. That way, isolated components just draw a negligible current to ground rather than breaking the solve, since the leak is small enough not to meaningfully affect the real current paths.

Building the Laplacian matrix...

Timing-wise each solve should take a couple hundred microseconds, so 600 evaluations lands around 0.2 seconds total, which is acceptable — though I could speed things up further by precomputing the fixed parts of the matrix structure ahead of time.

I'll skip scipy and stick with numpy for the solver. For scoring, I'm defining the metric as the log-resistance difference between my chain and the opponent's, computed by flipping and transposing the board to get the opponent's cell layout. Then I'm sketching the main policy function that builds the board state and handles the trivial empty-board case by returning the center move.

For move selection I'm laying out the priority order: first check for an immediate winning move by testing each empty cell, then check if the opponent has a winning threat and block it (either the single blocking cell or the best-scoring one among multiple threats), then fall back to one-ply evaluation. For the win-checking logic I'm writing a generic BFS-based connectivity check that works for either player by checking top-to-bottom connectivity on the board or its transpose depending on whose turn it is.

Since a winning move already scores as effectively infinite in the evaluation, explicit win/block checks are mostly a safety net against pruning errors in deeper search, so I'm keeping them cheap rather than relying purely on multi-ply search. I also want a fallback to any empty cell if nothing else applies, and to convert the final move back to the original color's coordinate convention before returning it.

For the two-ply search I'm scoring every possible move I could make and every possible reply the opponent could make, then narrowing to the top few candidates on each side by score to keep the search tractable, and for each of my candidate moves I evaluate the worst-case outcome across the opponent's plausible replies.

Now I'm setting a time budget so if evaluation runs too long, it falls back to the best move found from the shallower one-ply search or whatever's been evaluated so far.

I'm double checking the resistance formula's numerical bounds and the hex neighbor offsets against a worked example to confirm adjacency is correct.

Setting up numpy and timing imports along with the board dimension constants...

Building the graph Laplacian...

Finishing the resistance calculation, guarding against near-zero current, then defining the evaluation function that computes log-resistance for both players by comparing the board to its rotated/negated version for the opponent's perspective.

I'm now writing a win-detection function that does a BFS/DFS from the top row to see if a player's stones connect top to bottom, then applying it exhaustively across all empty cells for both orientations, checking that the performance cost stays manageable.

Writing policy function...

I'll pick the best-scoring move if there are multiple threats or if I'm running low on time. Otherwise, I'm computing opponent responses to narrow down candidate replies, then setting up a limited two-ply search over the top moves to find a stronger choice.

If time runs out early I'll fall back to the 1-ply best move, but if I've evaluated a few candidates before timing out, I'll use the best among those instead since the ordering already favors strong moves. I should also double-check the timing budget since root evaluation with these repeated solves could be more expensive than expected.

Multi-threat situations for the opponent are already handled by blocking whichever threat scores best, and my own winning check runs before any blocking logic so that's covered. One thing to verify is indexing tuples correctly into the board array and making sure the transpose-and-ravel trick for reading columns actually produces a contiguous copy in the right order.

Timing-wise, I'm estimating around 400µs per position evaluation, so a root search checking roughly 240 positions comes to about 100ms, well within budget — I can afford to widen the search to K=8 candidate moves with 10-15 replies each and still stay under 50ms, with a hard timeout guard at 0.8s as a safety net. Now I just need to write up the final answer describing the strategy.
